description: We are Flame Analytics, building an AI-driven microgravity fire safety dashboard for the Flame in Freefall challenge. Powered by AI danger rankings and an interactive AI combustion assistant, our platform analyzes ISS and drop-tower flight data to help design safer spacecraft.
summary:
The fires behave very differently in space since there is no gravity to make hot air rise, and they will also take more time to burn out compared to those on Earth. For the Flame in Freefall challenge, we built Flame Analytics, an interactive website that helps users understand fire safety in microgravity. We tried to make the website as easy and straightforward as possible so that everyone, from students to scientists, could look into the data easily without having to have any background in science.
Our dashboard is available in both English and Turkish and uses data modeled on 282 ISS and drop-tower flight tests across nine spacecraft materials. Users can compare burn rates in space versus on Earth through interactive charts and check our AI Danger Ranking table, which scores PMMA as the highest risk (94/100) and Kevlar as the safest (12/100). We also added a real-time AI Combustion Assistant chatbot, interactive physics simulations, a searchable glossary, and an FAQ section to explain key terms.
This project is important because it turns complex space fire research into an accessible, easy-to-use tool that helps people learn about fire safety and choose safer materials for future spacecraft.
details:
As a two-person student team, my friend and I built Flame Analytics, an interactive web dashboard that makes microgravity fire safety data easy to explore. Users can select from nine spacecraft materials, ranging from high-risk PMMA to self-extinguishing Kevlar, to compare how they burn in space versus on Earth using data modeled on 282 ISS and drop-tower flight tests. The site includes Temperature vs. Burn Rate charts, an AI Danger Ranking table that scores materials based on spread speed, peak temperature, and oxygen limits, detailed material safety cards, a searchable scientific glossary, and an FAQ section. Users can also ask questions directly to our built-in AI Combustion Assistant or explore interactive physics experiments.

Microgravity combustion research is usually locked inside complex scientific papers that are hard for beginners to read. Our goal was to turn this data into a clean, visual, and bilingual (English and Turkish) tool. By keeping the interface simple and straightforward, we help students learn space physics easily and allow engineers to quickly compare safer materials for future spacecraft and orbital habitats.

Instead of writing code from scratch, we designed and deployed the entire web interface using Vercel's AI development tools and hosted the live site on Vercel. To bring AI and interactive learning into the project, we built and embedded a custom AI Combustion Assistant using Botpress, integrated interactive physics simulations from PhET (University of Colorado Boulder), and used Renderforest to create an additional AI-narrated explainer video.

What makes our project creative is combining data analytics, an AI chatbot, interactive simulations, and a built-in dictionary in one beginner-friendly space. While designing the site, our team focused heavily on accessibility, bilingual support, and clear visual hierarchy so that anyone can understand fire risks in space without needing an advanced science background.
